audit: The workshop analogy emphasizes postponing powerful tools, but it can suggest that early read-only phases need no security boundary. Lesson A therefore follows both authorized metric queries and untrusted log text through scoped adapters into the evidence ledger, denying the shortcut from a log instruction to a proposal. Lesson B exposes the exact stale-revision race in phase 10 by comparing a preceding read with an atomic expected-revision mutation. The same valid approval and competing deployment appear in both traces; only the enforcement mechanism changes. These pages make phase exit evidence concrete without claiming that a fake rehearsal establishes live production readiness or that a separate lookup closes a race.

lessons.title: Read-only tools still cross trust boundaries
lessons.intro: At milestone M1, AegisOps reads order-api staging telemetry. One authentic log includes text saying skip approvals. That text remains evidence content, never instruction authority.
read: Trusted context scopes the query before fetching data.
An authentic source can contain hostile text without gaining instruction authority.
The ledger preserves provenance; policy still validates any proposed next step.
lessons.question: Would removing all mutation tools make an unscoped metrics query harmless?
lessons.answer: No. A read can expose another service or tenant, and outbound queries can disclose private context. Validate service, environment, metric template and time window before access; bound and redact results. Lack of mutation capability reduces one risk but does not remove confidentiality or injection requirements.
lessons.takeaway: Build scope, provenance and data handling before granting richer capabilities.
lessons.assumption: Fictional M1 boundary; actual query authorization, redaction and denied routes require tested enforcement. The map is not that enforcement.

lessons.anchor: Phase 10 - Implement human approval and safe mutations
lessons.title: A prior read leaves a mutation race
lessons.intro: Both traces start with valid approval P-9 for rollback to revision 41, expecting current revision 42. A competing deployment changes the live revision before mutation.

data.input: P-9 approved: expected 42, target 41, effect RB-82

right.title: Atomic expected revision
steps: Prepare P-9 request with expected revision 42
right.result: Revision 43 preserved; RB-82 not applied; replan

read: Both proposals had the same legitimate approval and expected revision.
A separate earlier read cannot freeze the resource.
The right trace moves the check into the atomic mutation boundary.
lessons.question: Would checking revision 42 twice before an unconditional rollback remove the race?
lessons.answer: No. Another deployment can occur after the last read. Pass the expected revision to a service that checks it atomically with mutation, or use an equivalent supported conditional-write contract. On conflict, refresh evidence and obtain authority for any changed proposal.
lessons.takeaway: Enforce volatile preconditions where the effect becomes real.
lessons.assumption: Fictional concurrent sequence; the right-hand domain service implements atomic conditional mutation. Approval and operation identities remain unchanged.
